brewing.notes: A safe starting point for green tea: cooler water, short steeps, then adjust by taste.

description:
A celebratory drink of the Kyoto and Kansai area, taken at New Year, Setsubun and on New Year's Eve; the New Year version is called obukucha. Sencha or plain hot water is poured over black soybeans, kombu, pickled plum and sansho.

Treat it as you would any green tea: cooler water, short steeps, and a seller who can say where and when it was picked.
history: By legend, the monk Kuya carried a carved Kannon through Kyoto during an epidemic in the reign of Emperor Murakami, and the sick who drank tea offered to it recovered, as did the emperor; he then took it each New Year's Day and the custom spread. Rokuharamitsu-ji temple dates Kuya's tea with plum and kombu to 951 and still gives it out over the first three days of the year. In the Omotesenke school the name goes to matcha made by the head of the school before dawn on New Year's Day.
processing: Assembled in the cup: sencha or hot water goes over black soybeans, kombu, pickled plum and sansho. For New Year it uses the year's first drawn water, and at Setsubun roasted soybeans are added.
harvest_season: Usually picked in spring, with the earliest pickings prized, as with most green teas.
appearance_dry: Green leaf whose shape depends on the maker, as is usual for regional green teas.
appearance_wet: Usually soft green leaf that opens up in the water.
taste_profile: Expect what green teas usually give: fresh, vegetal and lightly sweet.
vintage_note: Green teas like this are normally sold as the current year's harvest and are best within a year of picking. It is not an ageing tea.
